nodes.description: Gastrointestinal nodal involvement by the ingestion route can present as abdominal lymphadenopathy, documented in paediatric tularemia case reports.

evidence.reference_title: A rare cause of abdominal lymphadenopathy--tularemia: report of two pediatric cases.
evidence.snippet: To the best of our knowledge, these are the firstly described abdominal lymphadenopathy cases from Turkey.

nodes.description: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone option for tularemia antimicrobial therapy, including ingestion-route disease.

evidence.reference_title: Systematic Review: Clinical Features, Antimicrobial Treatment, and Outcomes of Human Tularemia, 1993-2023.
evidence.snippet: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and tetracyclines are effective antimicrobials for treatment of tularemia, regardless of clinical manifestation.

nodes.description: Innate immune activation after ingested F. tularensis produces inflammatory disease of the alimentary tract and abdominal lymph nodes, presenting rarely as abdominal lymphadenopathy.

evidence.reference_title: A rare cause of abdominal lymphadenopathy--tularemia: report of two pediatric cases.
evidence.snippet: It is necessary to consider tularemia in the differential diagnosis of abdominal lymphadenopathy in tularemia regions.

nodes.description: Enteric tularemia shares the acute febrile systemic illness seen across tularemia clinical forms.

evidence.reference_title: A rare cause of abdominal lymphadenopathy--tularemia: report of two pediatric cases.
evidence.snippet: It generally presents as an acute febrile disease with the major clinical presentations including the six classic forms of tularemia: ulceroglandular, glandular, oculoglandular, oropharyngeal, typhoidal, and pneumonic.

nodes.description: F. tularensis is ingested and contacts the gastrointestinal mucosa, establishing the enteric portal of entry that defines gastrointestinal tularemia.

evidence.reference_title: Bichat guidelines for the clinical management of tularaemia and bioterrorism-related tularaemia.
evidence.snippet: Seven clinical forms, according to route of inoculation (skin, mucous membranes, gastrointestinal tract, eyes, respiratory tract), dose of the inoculum and virulence of the organism (types A or B) are identified.

nodes.description: F. tularensis uses its Francisella Pathogenicity Island-encoded type VI secretion system to escape the macrophage phagosome and replicate in the cytosol.

evidence.reference_title: The Francisella tularensis pathogenicity island encodes a secretion system that is required for phagosome escape and virulence.
evidence.snippet: VgrG and IglI are required for F. tularensis phagosomal escape, intramacrophage growth, inflammasome activation and virulence in mice.

evidence.reference_title: The Francisella tularensis pathogenicity island encodes a secretion system that is required for phagosome escape and virulence.
